arml-2001-power-01a.title: Direct
arml-2001-power-01a.body: For $T=T(a,a,a)$ we have $T^2=T(a^2,a^2,a^2)$. Three equal positive sides satisfy the triangle inequality, so $T^2$ exists and is equilateral. ∎

arml-2001-power-01b.title: Triangle inequality fails
arml-2001-power-01b.body: Let $T=T(a,b,c)$ be a right triangle, so $a^2+b^2=c^2$ ($c$ is the hypotenuse, the largest side). The square would have sides $a^2,b^2,c^2$ with $c^2\ge b^2\ge a^2$, and the triangle inequality requires $a^2+b^2>c^2$. But $a^2+b^2=c^2$, so the inequality fails (the three lengths would be degenerate). Hence $T^2$ does not exist. ∎

arml-2001-power-02.title: Heron's formula
arml-2001-power-02.body:
With semi-perimeter $1+\frac x2$, Heron's formula gives $K(T)=\sqrt{\left(1+\frac x2\right)\left(1-\frac x2\right)\left(\frac x2\right)\left(\frac x2\right)}=\dfrac x4\sqrt{4-x^2}$ (valid for $0<x<2$). Replacing $x$ by $x^2$ and the equal sides $1$ by $1$: $K(T^2)=\dfrac{x^2}4\sqrt{4-x^4}$ (need $x^2<2$).

Set them equal: $\sqrt{4-x^2}=x\sqrt{4-x^4}$. Squaring, $4-x^2=x^2(4-x^4)$, i.e. $x^6-5x^2+4=0$. With $u=x^2$: $u^3-5u+4=(u-1)(u^2+u-4)=0$, so $u=1$ or $u=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}$ (the other root is negative). Both satisfy $0<u<2$, so $T$ and $T^2$ exist.

Hence $x=1$ or $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt{17}-1}{2}}$. ∎

arml-2001-power-03a.title: Law of Cosines
arml-2001-power-03a.body: $T^2=T(a^2,b^2,c^2)$ exists iff the triangle inequality holds; since $a^2\le b^2\le c^2$ the only condition is $a^2+b^2>c^2$. By the Law of Cosines $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$, so $a^2+b^2>c^2\iff 2ab\cos C>0\iff 0^\circ<C<90^\circ$. Since $C$ is the largest angle of $T$, this holds iff all angles are acute. ∎

arml-2001-power-03b.title: Triangle inequality for the roots
arml-2001-power-03b.body: We need $\sqrt a\le\sqrt b\le\sqrt c$ (clear) and $\sqrt a+\sqrt b>\sqrt c$. Now $(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^2=a+b+2\sqrt{ab}>a+b>c$, and taking square roots gives $\sqrt a+\sqrt b>\sqrt c$. ∎

arml-2001-power-04a.title: Largest angle
arml-2001-power-04a.body: Let $\theta$ be the angle of $\sqrt T$ opposite its largest side $\sqrt c$. By the Law of Cosines, $c=a+b-2\sqrt{ab}\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{a+b-c}{2\sqrt{ab}}>0$ because $a+b>c$. Thus the largest angle is acute, so all angles are acute. ∎

arml-2001-power-04b.title: Largest angle is at least $60^\circ$
arml-2001-power-04b.body: $A\le C$ and $B\le C$, so $180^\circ=A+B+C\le3C$, hence $C\ge60^\circ$ and $\cos C\le\cos60^\circ=\frac12$ (cosine is decreasing on $[0^\circ,180^\circ]$). Equality needs $A=B=C=60^\circ$, i.e. $T$ equilateral; conversely an equilateral triangle has $C=60^\circ$. ∎

arml-2001-power-05.title: Compare cosines
arml-2001-power-05.body:
Both largest angles are at least $60^\circ$ by 4(b), so being closer to $60^\circ$ means being smaller, i.e. having the larger cosine. For $T=T(a,b,c)$ and $T^2=T(a^2,b^2,c^2)$,
$$\cos C_T-\cos C_{T^2}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}-\frac{a^4+b^4-c^4}{2a^2b^2}=\frac{a^3b+ab^3-abc^2-a^4-b^4+c^4}{2a^2b^2}.$$
The numerator factors as $(c^2+b^2-ab)(c^2-b^2)+a^3(b-a)$. Since $c\ge b\ge a>0$: $c^2+b^2-ab>0$, $c^2-b^2\ge0$, $b-a\ge0$, so the numerator is $\ge0$. Therefore $\cos C_T\ge\cos C_{T^2}$, so $C_T\le C_{T^2}$, and both are $\ge60^\circ$. ∎

arml-2001-power-06a.title: Triangle inequality twice
arml-2001-power-06a.body: $X_n$ is a triangle iff $(n-1)+n>n+1$, i.e. $n>2$ (and $n>1$ for positive sides). Its square has sides $(n-1)^2,n^2,(n+1)^2$, and the only condition is $(n-1)^2+n^2>(n+1)^2\iff n^2-4n>0\iff n>4$ (using $n>0$). For $n>4$ both $X_n$ and $X_n^2$ exist. So the answer is all $n>4$. ∎

arml-2001-power-06b.title: Second squaring
arml-2001-power-06b.body:
$X_n$ can be squared twice iff $(X_n^2)^2=T\bigl((n-1)^4,n^4,(n+1)^4\bigr)$ exists, i.e. $(n-1)^4+n^4>(n+1)^4$. Since $(n+1)^4-(n-1)^4=8n^3+8n$, this reads $n^4-8n^3-8n>0$, i.e. $R(n)=n^3-8n^2-8>0$ for $n>0$.

$R(8)=-8<0$ and $R(9)=729-648-8=73>0$, so $R$ has a zero $k$ between $8$ and $9$. For $n>9$, $R(n)>n^3-8n^2-n^2=n^2(n-9)>0$; on $[k,9]$ $R$ is increasing and positive after the zero (its derivative $3n^2-16n>0$ for $n>6$). So for all $n\ge k$ (with $8<k<9$), $X_n$ can be squared twice, and $p=8$.

**Answer: $p=8$**

arml-2001-power-07a.title: Take roots of a right triangle
arml-2001-power-07a.body: $T_0=T(3,4,5)$ is a right triangle, so by 1(b) it cannot be squared. By 3(b), square roots of triangles always exist, so we can take $2001$ successive square roots: $T=T\bigl(3^{1/2^{2001}},4^{1/2^{2001}},5^{1/2^{2001}}\bigr)$. Squaring $T$ gives back the previous root, and so on; after $2001$ squarings we reach $T_0$ — each step is possible, because each is a square root of a valid triangle. A further squaring would square $T_0$, which is impossible. So $T$ can be squared exactly $2001$ times. ∎

arml-2001-power-07b.title: Compare the two largest sides
arml-2001-power-07b.body:
*Sufficient:* if $T=T(a,b,b)$ with $a\le b$, then the $k$-fold square is $T(a^{2^k},b^{2^k},b^{2^k})$ and both $a^{2^k}+b^{2^k}>b^{2^k}$ and $b^{2^k}+b^{2^k}>a^{2^k}$ hold, so it can be squared forever.

*Necessary:* suppose $T=T(a,b,c)$ with $c>b$. Then $(c/b)^{2^k}\to\infty$, so for large $k$ we have $c^{2^k}>2b^{2^k}\ge a^{2^k}+b^{2^k}$, and the $k$-fold square fails the triangle inequality. Hence $N(T)<\infty$.

So $N(T)=\infty$ exactly for isosceles triangles whose two equal sides are the two longer sides ($b=c$), i.e. $T(a,b,b)$ with $a\le b$; equivalently the base angles are at least $60^\circ$. ∎

arml-2001-power-08a.title: Two-term lemma, then three terms
arml-2001-power-08a.body:
*Lemma.* If $p,q,m$ are positive integers with $\sqrt p+\sqrt q=m$, then $p$ and $q$ are perfect squares. Indeed $\sqrt q=m-\sqrt p$, so $q=m^2-2m\sqrt p+p$, giving $\sqrt p=\dfrac{m^2+p-q}{2m}\in\mathbb Q$; an integer with a rational square root is a perfect square. By symmetry the same holds for $q$.

Now let $\sqrt a+\sqrt b=n-\sqrt c$. Squaring: $a+b+2\sqrt{ab}=n^2-2n\sqrt c+c$, so $2\sqrt{ab}+2n\sqrt c=n^2+c-a-b\in\mathbb Z$, i.e. $\sqrt{4ab}+\sqrt{4n^2c}$ is an integer. By the lemma $4n^2c$ is a perfect square, hence $c$ is a perfect square. The roles of $a,b,c$ are symmetric, so $a$ and $b$ are perfect squares too. ∎

arml-2001-power-08b.title: Reduce to $x^4+y^4=z^4$
arml-2001-power-08b.body: If the perimeter $\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c$ of $\sqrt T$ is an integer, then by 8(a) $a=x^2$, $b=y^2$, $c=z^2$ with positive integers $x,y,z$. The right-triangle condition $a^2+b^2=c^2$ becomes $x^4+y^4=z^4$, which has no solution in positive integers by Fermat's Last Theorem. ∎

arml-2001-power-09.title: Intermediate Value Theorem
arml-2001-power-09.body:
For $0<x\le1$ let $T_x=T\bigl(x,1,\sqrt{1+x^2}\bigr)$, a right triangle (the sides satisfy $x\le1\le\sqrt{1+x^2}$ and $x+1>\sqrt{1+x^2}$). Then $\sqrt{T_x}=T\bigl(\sqrt x,1,(1+x^2)^{1/4}\bigr)$ exists by 3(b), and
$$f(x)=P(T_x)-P(\sqrt{T_x})=(x-\sqrt x)+\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}-(1+x^2)^{1/4}\right),$$
a continuous function. Numerically $f(0.7)\approx-0.0208<0$ and $f(0.8)\approx0.0546>0$, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is $x\in(0.7,0.8)$ (about $0.7286$) with $f(x)=0$. For that $x$, the right triangle $T_x$ has the same perimeter as $\sqrt{T_x}$. ∎

arml-2001-power-09.title: Scaling a fixed right triangle
arml-2001-power-09.body: Let $T_1=T(1,1,\sqrt2)$ and let $T_t=T(1/t,1/t,\sqrt2/t)$ be its scaling by $1/t$, a right triangle. Then $P(T_t)=\dfrac{2+\sqrt2}{t}$ and $P(\sqrt{T_t})=\dfrac{2+\sqrt[4]{2}}{\sqrt t}$. At $t=1$, $P(T_1)-P(\sqrt{T_1})=\sqrt2-\sqrt[4]2>0$. At $t=4$, $P(T_4)=\dfrac{2+\sqrt2}{4}<\dfrac{2+\sqrt[4]2}{2}=P(\sqrt{T_4})$ (since $2+\sqrt2<4+2\sqrt[4]{2}$). The difference is continuous in $t$, so it vanishes for some $t\in(1,4)$ (about $1.146$). ∎

arml-2001-power-10.title: Normalize by $c$
arml-2001-power-10.body:
Put $x=\dfrac ac$, $y=\dfrac bc$, so $0<x\le y\le1$. $T$ being a triangle gives $x+y>1$, i.e. $y>1-x$. $T^{-1}$ being a triangle requires $\dfrac1c+\dfrac1b>\dfrac1a$; multiplying by $c$: $1+\dfrac1y>\dfrac1x$.

If $x=1$ there is nothing to prove ($1>\frac{3-\sqrt5}2$). Otherwise $0<1-x<y$ and $\dfrac1x<1+\dfrac1y<1+\dfrac1{1-x}=\dfrac{2-x}{1-x}$. Hence $1-x<x(2-x)$, i.e. $x^2-3x+1<0$, so $x$ lies strictly between the roots $\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}2$. In particular $x>\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}2$, i.e. $a>\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}2\,c$. ∎
